item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports separating transient intent from persistent preferences with adaptive fusion. [TLSTSRec (online 2024; volume 2025)](https://doi.org/10.3233/IDA-240051) combines long- and short-term temporal information through trainable timestamp representations and personalized fusion layers. [Multi-Scale Transformers (2026)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0306457325002596) uses dual attention for transient and stable interests, with adaptive masking to reduce redundant interactions. Earlier, directly relevant [TLSRec (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04760) introduced time-lag-sensitive fusion of hierarchical long- and short-term preferences. These provide architectural precedents; they do not establish gains on the four pinned Amazon categories.\n\nPractical hypothesis for SASRec: retain its causal sequence representation, add a recent-window branch and a pooled historical-preference branch, then learn a sigmoid gate conditioned on both representations, observed inter-event gaps and history length. A small learned decay over log-scaled elapsed times is a reasonable ablation, rather than an established result from these papers. [TSAPE (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3774904.3792333) offers another lightweight direction: adaptive temporal positional encoding integrated into SASRec. For sparse histories, compare gating against simple pooling and fixed mixtures to determine whether added parameters help. Compute every temporal feature from the available history prefix; without a known prediction timestamp, anchor elapsed times to its latest interaction. Select using the unchanged macro validation HR@10. Interaction timing supports relevance modeling, but does not establish ownership, replacement needs or unobserved user traits."}
